entries.text:
Brannoc is at 1 HP with no spells. Cal is dead beside him, Hob can't leave the lamp, and two ghouls are still loose in the woods. It's just past midnight on Day 2. The lamp burns on the pony's oil until grey light.

Hob has told you what he knows. He can't stray more than a few hundred paces from the lamp. The flagstone is the lid of an old stair to a burial place beneath the shrine, and he knows no other way up.

You can carry Cal home on a litter, which means a mile of dark beechwood alone, or wait by the lamp to recover first. What does Brannoc do?

Hob lifts his head, and the dull coin-eyes follow your hand to the coat. "...Cal," he says, as if learning the name. "Good hunter. He walked my track... since he was a boy. I left apples on the step for him."

He answers your questions slowly, a few words at a time.

"The lamp... will burn till grey light. The pony's oil... and what he carried. I must stay near it. A few hundred paces, no more. Further, and I... come apart." He turns the unlit lantern in his hands. "Tonight I walked a mile for you. It cost me."

"The stones... there is a stair. Old. Older than my shrine. It goes down to a burial place, and the flagstone is the lid. I never knew another way up. I never looked." His head tilts. "They hate this light. But two are out in the hills. They'll come back to the hole before dawn, or they won't. If the lamp is dark when they do..."

He does not finish.

The track south is a mile of dark beechwood with two ghouls somewhere in it, and you are at 1 HP with no spells and a body to carry. A litter of two branches and Cal's coat would work, and Hob can't leave the light, so you would carry him alone. The alternative is to wait here by the lamp until you have recovered, at the cost of Wil's fever and the barn's long night.

You also have a quiet minute to think, and a choice to make about what Cal's family will want you to bring back: him, or only word of him.

entries.text:
You kneel stiffly and lay your hand on the coat over Cal. Hob waits until you finish. When he speaks, the words come more easily than before, as if the lamp's light is loosening something in him.

"The lamp... holds while there is oil, and I am near. I am bound to it. If I go from it, it dims." He looks at the pale lantern in his lap. "There is oil in the dead pony's packs. Enough to burn... until well past dawn. In daylight they will not climb. They sleep deep."

On the other way up, he is slow to answer. "The stones above are the only door I know. But the under-dark is old and wide. Older than my shrine. I built on a cellar I never dared to open. There may be other mouths. Hungry ones have gone out toward the village by some road. Two of them... did not come up through this floor."

That last part is worth thinking about.

Cal's body is a hard matter for someone at 1 HP. A bowman's frame is heavy, and the mile is mostly downhill but dark and muddy. The pony's torn packs have canvas and rope, enough for a drag-litter, and there is a stout hazel pole you could use. Carrying him will be slow, and you will arrive near dawn, which is exactly when you wanted to be back for Wil. You can also take Cal home properly after dawn, once you've seen to the living, and leave him here under the lamp's light and Hob's watch.

Your spells are gone and you have 1 HP. Hob offers a quiet suggestion: "Rest... an hour by the lamp. You will not be harmed here." A short rest would let you spend your hit die. A long rest is the only thing that would restore your prayers, and it needs eight hours, which is more than the night leaves.

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for Who Opened the Barrow

I wrote the scene above before I recorded it, and I should have recorded it first. The clock now reads Day 2, 12:05 AM. The notebook now has the barrow under the Lamp and a lead for finding out who pried it open.

Brannoc is at 1 HP with no spells. He can rest in the Lamp's light, or he can build a litter for Cal and head down the track. What does he do?

You lay your hand on the coat over Cal and say his name, and Hob bows his head beside you. Nothing moves in the clearing but the lamplight.

Hob answers slowly, and the words come a little easier than before. "The lamp holds... while there is oil. Pony's flasks. Enough till dawn. Past dawn... I must tend it. I cannot leave it. Not again." His cracked fingers close on his lantern. "Another way up? I do not know of one. Under the stones is an old barrow, older than the lamp. I kept the slab shut forty years. At harvest... someone came with an iron bar. I remember the bar. I remember nothing after."

When you look at the dragged flagstone by the light, you see fresh pry-marks bright in the old mortar, made from above. Something that crawls up from below did not do this. Someone opened that barrow, and the hungry ones came out after.

The practical facts are these. You have 1 HP, no spells, and a mile of dark beechwood between you and the barn, with two ghouls still loose on that side. The lamp's light is safe, and you could rest here in it. You are in no state to carry a grown man a mile, but Cal's blanket and two beech poles would make a litter you could drag. Wil's fever is not going to wait for a rested cleric.

input.add_to_description: Day 1 midnight: Hob, undead but gentle, is bound to the lamp and must stay near it to keep it fed. Says the lamp will burn until dawn on the oil he has; the ghouls came from a crypt-stair under the flagstone, which he knows of no other way out of, but the two roaming ones are outside and will return to the stone before sunrise. He offers the pony's blanket and two lamp-house poles for a litter to carry Cal home.

entries.text:
You kneel by Cal in the lamplight, your hand on the coat, and say his name and your promise aloud. The hymn comes without your deciding it, low and a little broken. Hob waits until you finish. He does not hurry you.

"The lamp will hold," he says, each word slow. "Oil enough... until dawn. I stay. I must. Where the light is... I am still myself." He looks at the flagstone, shut tight beneath the plinth. "They came up from a stair below. Old. Older than the lamp. I know no other way up. But two are loose in the dark... and they will come back to the stone before the sun. They do not like the day."

His dull eyes turn to the pony's torn pack. "There is a blanket. Two poles, inside. You could carry him... the track is downhill. Slow."

Your own state is plain. You are on 1 HP, with no prayers left in you, your armor heavy and your hands unsteady. The track runs a mile through the beechwoods, and two ghouls are somewhere in them. The lamp throws a warm circle about fifty feet wide, and everything beyond it is black. In the barn, Wil's fever is climbing, and the people there are counting on you by first light.

You could rest here in the lamp's circle, Hob keeping watch, and go down in an hour or two with a little strength back. You could set out now with Cal on a litter and take the risk in the dark. Or you could do something I haven't thought of. What does Brannoc do?

You sit at her table, and you hold the bow out in both hands, as you said you would. You tell her all of it: that he went because he was asked, that he knew the track and led it, that the oil plan was his to throw and he threw it true, that he never turned back. You don't hide that it was quick, and that Hob could not save him. You tell her that you said the prayer over him, and that the lamp lit his face.

She says nothing for a long time. Then she takes the bow, runs her thumb along the string-groove, and sets it across her knees. "He strung it himself, the winter he was fourteen," she says. "Cut the stave from an ash by the wash. Said it'd shoot true." Her mouth trembles once and steadies. "He did."

She asks about the rota when you raise it, and her answer is firm. "Put his name on it. Oil and candles, from this house, every week as long as I've hands to carry them. And I'd have the bow hang by that Lamp's door, where he went." You say you will carry it up. She nods. When you mention Maud in Greywater, she gives you a small, tired smile. "Tell her Hob kept the road for her too. She never knew how many it saved."

You sit with her until noon, and she gives you bread and a cup of cold water, and you hum Edda's hymn quietly while she eats nothing. It is half past eleven now. You are at full strength, with all three prayers, Channel Divinity, and the powder for Protection from Evil and Good. Cal's bow is in his mother's hands, ready to hang at the Lamp's door.

The road ahead has three pulls. You could walk up to the Lamp with the bow and Pell and Dorrin to set the first watch, which would fit before dusk. You could set out for Greywater, a day's walk down the valley, to tell Maud. Or you could stay in the Reach a while longer and help the wounded and the grieving.

The last house on the lane is small and neat, with a swept step and a bundle of drying herbs by the door. You knock softly. After a long moment the door opens on a woman with Cal's quick dark eyes, gone red-rimmed and very still. She looks at your amulet, and at the bow in your hands, and says nothing. Then she steps back and lets you in.

Insight (19): you read her at once. She doesn't need comfort so much as to know that someone saw it. She has spent two days imagining the worst, and she wants it plain.

You sit by her cold hearth and give it to her straight. Cal came because he was asked. He led you up the track in the dark, knew every bend of it, and he stood his ground against two ghouls with a bow and a lit jar of oil. He never once turned back. You tell her the oil plan was his to throw and that it worked, and that the lamp was lit because he bought the time. You hold the bow out in both hands, and she takes it the way one takes a sleeping child. Her fingers find the worn place on the stave where his hand sat, and she presses her mouth to it and doesn't make a sound for a long while.

When she speaks, her voice is rough. "He ran hares on that track since he was nine. I told him the woods would take him someday." She almost smiles. "He'd have said it was the best-lit road in the county." She wipes her face with her sleeve. "Put his name on the rota. Put it first. Let the Lamp burn for him." Then, after a moment: "Greywater. You'll carry word to Hob's sister? Tell her he kept faith. That's a thing worth knowing."

You stay an hour, until she is calm enough to sit alone, and you leave the house in the thin noon light with the lane quiet around you. The longbow is gone from your pack.

It is half past ten. You have your prayers and your powder, the rota is half-built, and the road to Greywater runs a day down the valley. Hob waits at the Lamp, and the ghouls wait under the stone.

The last house on the lane is small and tidy, with a swept step and a hare-skin pegged out to dry beside the door. You knock softly and wait. The door opens on a small, spare woman with Cal's quick dark eyes, red-rimmed and dry. She looks at your face, and then at the bow in your hands, and she steps back and lets you in.

You sit with her at a table scrubbed pale. You don't leave out that he died. She listens without interrupting. When you finish she takes the bow and lays it across her knees and runs her thumb down the grip, worn smooth by his hand.

"He ran hares up there since he was nine," she says at last. "I told him the Lamp was haunted. He said the Lamp was the only honest light on the road." Her mouth trembles and steadies. "I'd like his name kept there. Not on a stone. In the oil. Every week I'll send a jar, and it'll be his."

The last house on the lane is small and neat, with a swept step and a hare-skin pegged to dry by the door. You knock softly and wait. She steps back, and you go in.

You tell her all of it. He knew the track since he was nine. He was the first to say he would go. He drew the bow in the dark and loosed arrow after arrow at a thing that wanted him dead, and he did not run. You tell her he was not alone, and that you held his hand afterward and spoke the old words over him. Nessa listens with her hands folded in her lap. When you reach the end, she nods once. It is nearly eleven when you step out again into the sun. You carry two things you hadn't before: a small carved wooden hare Nessa pressed into your hand, Cal's first knife-work, and her message for Maud Marrow.

Your tasks now: the Lamp's rota is half set, Greywater lies a day's walk down the valley with word for Maud, and the barrow below still holds three ghouls under the slab. What does Brannoc do?

input.add_to_description: Day 4 ~9:30 AM: Brannoc reached her blue-doored loom-house in Greywater and delivered Hob's message and the blue shawl. Sharp-tongued, grey-braided, mid-fifties; had not heard from Hob since midsummer and feared the worst. Wants to see the Lamp herself.
Day 4 ~9:30 AM: word of Hob delivered to Maud in Greywater, with the shawl. Quest complete except Maud's own decision to visit the Lamp.

entries.text: sheet: lost 1 × Blue shawl (Maud Marrow's, to return to her); XP +50: 350

The girl with the yarn points with her chin and says, "Maud? The blue door, down by the weir. She's up already, she's always up." She watches you go, and by the time you reach the lower lane she has told two others, and a few shutters have eased open.

You walk with your shield slung on your back and your hands open at your sides. The loom-house is narrow and old, its blue paint worn pale. Through the window you hear the steady clack and thump of a loom. It stops when you knock.

Maud Marrow opens the door herself. She is a spare, upright woman in her middle fifties with a gray braid down her back, wool-lint on her apron and dye-stained fingers, and she has Hob's long jaw. Her sharp eyes go from your mace to your amulet and then to your face, and you see her understand before you say a word.

"My name is Brannoc," you say. "I come from Hob. May I come in? I've something of yours, and I'd like to tell you about him in my own words."

She stands quite still. Then she says, very evenly, "He's dead." It is not a question. "I've known since midsummer, when he didn't write. Come in, then."

You sit at her table, and you tell her all of it: the Lamp gone dark, the ghouls under the stones, how he walked the road at night for lanterns and could not speak until he heard a hymn, how he lit the Lamp at last and held the dark back, and that he still keeps it. Then you say his words, one at a time, exactly as he said them. That he kept the light. That he was not afraid, at the end. That the shawl was warm, every night. You take it from your pack, faded blue, smelling of lamp smoke, and lay it in her hands.

She holds it against her face for a long moment without a sound. When she lowers it, her eyes are dry and fierce and wet at once. "Somewhere to be," she says hoarsely, at the last line. "Of course he did. Stubborn old goat. Forty years, and he never once came home for the harvest." A short, cracked laugh breaks out of her. "I'd have told him to come home."

She asks what you ask of her, nothing; you ask nothing. She says she will walk to the Lamp, three days' road, to see it with her own eyes, and she will bring wool for the keepers' blankets and her loom's share of oil every winter for as long as she lives. Then she insists you eat, and she will not be argued with.

It is mid-morning. You earned 50 XP for carrying the word faithfully, and you stand at 350 of the 900 you need for level 3. The Lamp Watch is done. Greywater has no priest, and a girl at the window is already whispering about the healer who has come. Several doors along the lane are cracked open.

entries.text:
The girl points without a word, then walks you to the end of the lane, the basket bumping her hip. She nods at the blue door and goes quickly back the way she came.

You swing the shield onto your back and knock. A loom is clacking inside, a steady rhythm, and it stops mid-pass. The door opens on a spare, bright-eyed woman of sixty or so, with gray hair under a kerchief and a shuttle still in her hand. Her eyes find the amulet, then your face, and she goes still, the way people do when they have been expecting a knock for a long time.

"Maud Marrow? My name is Brannoc, and I come from Hob. May I come in? I have something of yours in my pack, and I'd like to tell you about him in my own words."

"Hob," she says. "You'd better come in." She doesn't ask whether he's alive. She steps aside.

The room is warm and bright, full of skeins in a dozen colors, with the loom under the window and the river loud outside. She sits you at the table and does not offer tea until you've said it. You tell it all, gently, in order: the lamp gone dark, the creatures from below, how he walked to the barn begging for light and could not make himself understood, how he spoke to you through a door, and how he led you to the Lamp and lit it with his own hands. You say he died before you ever met him, but that he stayed, because the light was his to keep. You do not lie, and you do not make it harder than it was.

She listens without a word, the shuttle turning slowly in her fingers. When you reach the end, you take the blue shawl from your pack and lay it across the table. She puts out a hand and touches it, faded now and smelling of lamp smoke. Her mouth works.

Then you give her his words, exactly: that he kept the light, that he was not afraid at the end, that the shawl was warm every night, and that she would say he should have come home. "And he said, 'Tell her I had somewhere to be.'"

Maud makes a sound that is half a laugh and half something else, and she covers her eyes. "That stubborn old goat," she says, wet and furious and fond. "Forty years I told him. Forty years." She sits with the shawl pressed to her face for a long while, and you sit with her, humming low, and say nothing at all. It is, you think, exactly what Edda would have done.

When she can speak again, she looks up, red-eyed and fierce. "He never wanted anyone to come after him. But somebody ought to. A keeper's got to have kin." She wipes her face on her sleeve. "I'll go up. I'll sit his watch myself, a month at a time, and I'll bring the wool. Will you tell them in the Reach?"

The shawl is hers again, the message is delivered, and the Lamp will have a keeper of blood as well as of habit. It is mid-morning. Greywater has a chapel with no priest, a weaver's village that might want a healer, and the road ahead goes on. What does Brannoc do?

She wipes her eyes with the heel of her hand. "I knew. I knew at the turn of the harvest, when no letter came. He never missed a letter."

When she can speak steadily again, she asks three things. She would like to see the Lamp herself, in a day or two, when she can close the loom-house. She will weave wicks and good cloth for the rota, for as long as it needs them. And Greywater has no priest of its own; she asks whether you would say words for Hob in the chapel, so that people who knew him can come.

It is about half past seven in the morning, and the whole village is waking up around you. You are rested and have all your prayers. What does Brannoc do?

The girl points with her chin, a little wary, and then softer when she sees your amulet. "Maud? Blue door, by the weir. She's up already. She's always up." She watches you go.

Maud Marrow is sixty or near it, narrow and brisk, with a gray braid down her back and fingertips stained deep blue to the first knuckle. She looks you up and down before you speak. When you say your name and that you come from Hob, her face does not change, but her hand tightens on the door. "Come in, then," she says. "Mind the warp."

Her house is all thread: skeins on pegs, a great loom under the window, a kettle ticking on a small stove. You do not take the chair she offers until she sits. You tell it plainly, in your own words: that her brother is dead, that he kept the lamp to the end and saved a village, that he was not afraid. You give her his message exactly as he gave it, including the last part. "He said you would tell him he should have come home. He said to tell you he had somewhere to be."

For a long moment she says nothing. Then she makes a short dry sound that is half a laugh. "Somewhere to be. The stubborn old goat." She presses the back of her wrist to her mouth. When you take the blue shawl from your pack and lay it in her hands, she holds it to her face and her shoulders go. You sit and hum, very low, and do not speak, and the loom stands silent. It is a long time before she looks up.

"Take me to him," she says. Her voice is rough but steady. "I'll not have him sitting alone on a step. A day's walk, you say? I've walked further for worse." She wipes her eyes with the heel of her hand. "And I'll be bringing lamp oil. I know what that old fool would forget."

You earn 100 XP for carrying the promise home, which brings you to 400 of the 900 needed for level 3. Maud is already pulling down a coat and stuffing a loaf in a bag. It is about half past nine on Day 4, and the road back to the Lamp is a day's walk.

entries.text:
The girl with the yarn basket points without a word toward the weir. She watches you go with the wide, careful eyes of someone who has seen a stranger's face and guessed the news on it.

The house with the blue door is narrow, with a loom clacking inside. You hang your shield on your back, and the clacking stops at your knock. The woman who opens is in her sixties, gray-haired and spare, with wool lint on her sleeves and her brother's long jaw. Her eyes go to your amulet and then to your face.

"Maud Marrow? My name is Brannoc, and I come from Hob. May I come in? I have something of yours in my pack, and I'd like to tell you about him in my own words."

She stands very still. "From Hob," she says. "Not with him." It is not a question. Then she steps back and holds the door. "Come in, then. Sit. I'll hear it standing."

You do not rush it. You tell her about the Lamp gone dark and the village locking its doors, the dead keeper at the barn door asking only for light, the four nights, the ghouls under the stones, and Hob lighting the flame with his own pale lantern. You tell her he is bound to the Lamp, that he was not afraid, and that he kept the light. Then you take the folded blue shawl from your pack and lay it in her hands, and give her his words exactly: that it was warm, every night, and that she is to have it back.

She says nothing for a long time. Her fingers move over the wool, finding the places she knows. Then, in a voice that is barely steadier than the weir: "He'd say I talk too much." A breath. "Did he say I'd tell him he should have come home?"

You say he did, and that he said he had somewhere to be.

Maud laughs once, short and broken, and puts the shawl to her face. When she lowers it, her eyes are wet and her mouth is set. "Forty years he kept that Lamp," she says. "I thought he'd just got old and stubborn. I never once asked what it was for." She looks at you. "I'll go up. Not today, I've two orders on the loom and a debt to the dyer. But I'll go, and I'll sit by that light, and I'll tell him what a fool he was." Her voice cracks. "Thank you for coming yourself. Nobody has done a kindness this size for me in a long time."

She puts the kettle on and will not hear of you leaving without a meal.

The errand is done: Hob's words are delivered and Cal's bow is home. It is mid-morning on Day 4, you are rested and at full strength with all your prayers, and the road goes on in every direction. Greywater has a chapel with no priest, and Maud mentions a few households with fevers and coughs. Hollow Reach would welcome you back, and the open road is yours.

entries.text:
The girl with the yarn points with her whole arm. "Maud? Blue door, by the weir. She's up. She's always up." She watches you go with round eyes.

You sling the shield across your back, which feels odd after so many days, and walk down between the drying racks, red and blue and ochre wool lifting in the thin wind. The weir roars white beside the lower lane. The house with the blue door is narrow and tall, with a loom's clacking coming through the shutters, steady as a heartbeat. You knock, and it stops.

The woman who opens the door is small and sharp-faced, with a gray braid down her back and Hob's pale, direct eyes. A shuttle is still in her hand. She looks at your amulet, your mace, your tired face, and she goes still. "You've come about Hob," she says. It is not a question.

You say what you planned: your name, that you come from him, that you have something of hers in your pack. She steps back and lets you in without another word. The room is full of looms and baskets of wool, and a kettle sings on the hearth. She sits you down and does not ask for tea, and you tell it in your own words, slowly and fully, as you promised.

You tell her he kept the light, that he saved a village by it, and that he never once harmed a soul. You tell her what he was at the end and what he asked of you, and then you take the blue shawl from your pack and put it in her hands. She sits holding it for a long time, thumb moving over the faded wool.

"I wove this the winter he went up there," she says at last. "I told him he was a fool. Forty years, alone, for strangers." She laughs, a small, wet, cracked sound. "Warm every night. Did he say that?" You tell her exactly what he said, word for word, including the last: that she talks too much, and that he had somewhere to be. She laughs again and wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist. "He was right on both counts."

She is quiet a while. Then she says, firmly, "I'm going up there. Today. I'll not leave him to strangers. I've a brother-in-law with a cart who'll take me, and I'll sit with him." She looks at you. "You'll come back with us? You know the track."

The Lamp Watch is done. You carried every word. The rest is a choice: go back with Maud to Hollow Reach and see the Lamp tended, or take the road onward from Greywater, where the valley opens toward other towns and other people with no healer.

You sit in her kitchen with a cup of tea you do not drink. She listens to all of it without interrupting: the lamp gone dark, the hungry ones, the keeper at the door, a dead man begging for light. Her jaw works at the part about the lanterns. When you say he was not afraid, she shuts her eyes. You give her his words exactly, down to the last, "Tell her I had somewhere to be." And at that she makes a sound halfway between a laugh and a sob. "Stubborn old goat," she says. "Forty years, and he still wouldn't write."

You lay the blue shawl in her hands. She unfolds it slowly, finds the place in one corner where the weave goes wrong, and runs her thumb over the flaw. "I made that the first winter he went. Dropped a stitch. He said he liked it." She holds it against her chest.

When she can speak again she says she wants to see the Lamp for herself, and the stone where he sat. She will go up to Hollow Reach with the next carter and take a turn at the wick. She presses a skein of undyed wool into your hands that she says will keep your shoulders warm, and walks you to the blue door. "You sat with a boy at the Millstone all night," she says. "I heard in the market. You're a long way from home, aren't you."

Greywater is quiet in the morning sun, and the road goes on in two directions, back up the valley or down toward the next town. A small chapel at the village edge stands shut, with no priest to tend it.

What does Brannoc do next?

entries.text:
The girl with the yarn basket points without a word, then follows a few steps behind you as you go. You sling your shield over your back so the mace and mail look less like a soldier's, and walk down between the drying racks to the house by the weir. The blue door has a worn brass knocker shaped like a shuttle. You knock twice.

The loom stops. The woman who opens the door is in her sixties, gray-braided and thin, with Hob's long jaw and sharp eyes, a shuttle still in one hand. She looks at your amulet, then at your face. You say your name, that you come from Hob, and that you have something of hers in your pack. She doesn't answer for a moment. Then she steps back. "Come in, then. I've been expecting someone."

Her workroom smells of lanolin and woad. The loom stands in the window, half a cloth on it, blue. She sits on the bench without being asked, and you sit across from her and tell it in your own words, slowly. You say how he kept the Lamp, how the lamp went dark and the dead came up, and how he walked down the track in the dark to beg a village for light and could not speak. You say how he stood in the lamp's glow with his lantern when you came, and kept it lit for a boy who died. Then you give her his words, exactly, all of them, down to "I had somewhere to be."

She laughs once at the last, a short, cracked sound, and puts her hand over her mouth. Then you take the shawl from your pack and hold it out. She doesn't take it at first. She looks at it a long time. "I wove this the winter he went up there," she says. "He said he didn't feel the cold. He lied." She takes it and holds it to her face.

When she can speak, she says, quietly, that he sent a letter at harvest-tide, a few lines, and that she had known by the handwriting that he was dying or dead. She had not wanted to go and be sure. She is not angry with you. She asks if the Lamp is still lit, and whether he is there, and when you say yes, she nods slowly. "Then I'll go up. Not today." She looks at the shawl. "He'll want his sister to sit with him a while. He always did, though he'd never say." She asks what she owes you, and you can see she means it.

It is half past nine. Greywater has no priest, and a chapel stands shut at the village's end. You are at full strength with every prayer, your message delivered, and your road open. What does Brannoc do?
